dossier: The Kallava Rule Leaf is a single palm-leaf strip bearing a short set of monastic regulations, found in 1987 beneath a collapsed shrine at the Kallava hillside settlement. The text concerns the sharing of alms, procedures for settling disputes, and the temporary suspension of a monk who leaves the residence during the rains. Its letters are in a western-Brahmi hand, uneven in size, with several forms also seen on locally excavated potsherds. The leaf is 31 centimetres long, pierced twice for binding, and darkened along one edge; abrasion crosses both the writing and the holes. A margin sample gave a broad radiocarbon range spanning the first centuries CE. However, the ink sits unusually evenly in the surface, and one rule uses a compound legal term absent from the other surviving Kallava fragments. A faint ruled grid beneath the text is visible only under angled light; its lines do not align consistently with the letters.

The Yulan Translation Register is a single-sheet record said to have been recovered from a sealed niche at the Qingsha Cliff Repository. It lists portions of a Mahāyāna scripture rendered into Chinese by the monk Fayan, with a brief note assigning the work to the third year of the Jinglu era. Most of the text is in regular script; the translator’s name and two corrections are in smaller, hurried clerical script. The sheet is pale brown, about the size of a modern folio, with a crease down the center, insect losses at one edge, and faint ruled lines. Its compact columns and formulaic dedication resemble formats described in records from the same period. Yet the title uses a translation term otherwise associated in the dossier’s setting with later centuries, and the unusually even spacing continues across a repaired strip. A dark stain obscures part of the date; the paper’s surface bears scattered, glossy fibers.

The Willow Bank Leaf is a single sheet bearing a poem attributed within the text to the otherwise Tang poet Lu Zhaoran. It was recorded as having been found in 1986 inside a collapsed storehouse wall at the Shuanghe Temple, near Longyou. The sheet is tawny, thin paper, folded once, with a torn lower edge and a pale rectangular stain where a label may have rested. Its twelve lines are written in dark ink in a quick, semi-cursive hand; several characters use forms also found in surviving Tang manuscripts, while others have unusually regular proportions. The poem describes a ferry at dusk and includes a place-name documented in local gazetteers. A small docket on the reverse gives a reign year and a copying date, but the reign title is written in a form associated with later clerical practice. The paper carries scattered fibers and insect channels, alongside two sharply cut holes that interrupt the final line.

The Veyr Abbey Annal Leaf is a single-page Latin chronicle entry, nominally dated to the year 1178, describing a flood, a market dispute, and the arrival of a visiting prior. It was recorded in the catalogue of the abbey of Saint Orra at Veyr after being found folded inside a seventeenth-century account book. The leaf measures roughly  twenty-four by sixteen centimetres and is cut from sheepskin, with hair follicles visible along one edge. Faint ruling lines and a small prick mark at the upper margin remain. Most of the text is in brown ink, in a compact Caroline-influenced book hand; several letter shapes and abbreviations resemble those in other Veyr records. A narrow passage, however, uses an unfamiliar form for the word “borough,” and the year’s feast-day notation appears inconsistent with the abbey’s surviving calendar. The final two lines are crowded into the lower margin, where a later hand added a short place-name in faded red ink.

The North Ford Almanac Leaf is a single printed sheet said to have been recovered in 1912 from a bricked recess beneath the Heshan post station. It carries a short notice about ferry tolls and market days, followed by a two-line colophon naming the third year of the Jingyou era. The text is cut in small regular script, with several characters printed unevenly and one narrow patch where the block seems to have shifted. Its gray-brown paper has visible plant fibers, a chain-line spacing, and a worn fold that crosses the printed columns; the ink has soaked into the sheet rather than sitting sharply on its surface. A faint brush correction appears beside one damaged character. However, the colophon uses a later-looking form of a tally mark, and the paper’s unusually even thickness contrasts with its ragged edge. A pale rectangle on the reverse may be an old mounting stain, though its borders are sharply defined. No printer’s name or surviving wrapper accompanies the leaf.

The Kōmyōji Granary Leaf is a single-page temple account, reportedly recovered in 1987 from a sealed storage niche beneath the floor of the Kōmyōji’s west storehouse. It records rice allotments, lamp oil, and repairs to a boundary ditch for the ninth month of 1468. The main text is in flowing kuzushiji, with a brief column of figures in a more formal hand; a vermilion seal names the temple’s steward, Jōen. The sheet is thin, cream-colored kōzo paper, with irregular fibers and a fold pattern consistent with long storage among bundled accounts. Soot staining darkens one edge, and the ink has feathered into the fibers. However, the date uses a reign-era form not otherwise found in the temple’s surviving registers, and one place-name appears in a spelling common in later copies. A narrow strip pasted along the bottom bears a different paper texture and obscures part of the final sum. No matching cover or attachment survives.

document_name: The Life of Saint Thekla of Nera
dossier: The Life of Saint Thekla of Nera survives on a single parchment bifolium reportedly uncovered in 1912 behind a blocked niche in the monastery of Saint Mamas, on the island of Lykara. Its compact Greek minuscule, with enlarged initials and occasional ligatures, resembles hands used in provincial books of the eleventh century; a faded quire mark and ruling pricks are also visible. The text recounts Thekla’s healing of a fevered boatman, her dispute with a local tax collector, and her death during a winter vigil. A short prayer at the end names a nearby spring whose cult is otherwise unattested. The parchment is unevenly trimmed and bears soot along one edge, while a water stain crosses several lines without obscuring them. Most ink is brown, but the final three lines are in a darker, slightly glossy ink. The feast date is written above the text in a different hand, using a title not found elsewhere in the narrative.

The Suryŏng Ridge Bell Inscription is a rubbing and surviving fragment attributed to a small temple bell from the late Silla–early Goryeo transition. It was reportedly found in 1978 near a collapsed stone platform on Suryŏng Ridge, wrapped in a layer of roof tile fragments. The text records a donor’s name, a short vow for the protection of the realm, and a dedication to the Buddha of Medicine. Most characters are written in a compact form of classical Chinese, with two vernacular glosses rendered in idu-style notation. The bronze fragment has a green-brown patina, shallow casting seams, and corrosion concentrated along its broken edge; traces of the inscription continue beneath one patch of mineral accretion. The rubbing, however, includes a crisp line absent from the fragment, and its paper bears a watermark associated with modern manufacture. A date formula uses an era name known from other transitional-period records, while one personal title appears in a form otherwise documented several centuries later. The fragment measures 19 by 11 centimeters and has a small drilled hole near one corner.

The Qasr al-Nur Register is a two-leaf paper document said to have been recovered from a sealed storeroom beneath a caravanserai near the oasis of Ayn Sahl. It records grain allocations and lamp-oil expenses for a small charitable endowment, with entries dated across three successive years in the late ninth century. Most of the text is in compact Arabic naskh, though the script’s early, upright forms sit uneasily beside several rounded letter shapes more typical of later hands. The brown ink has bled into the fibers in places, and a faint offset on the facing leaf suggests the pages were once folded together. A short devotional phrase appears in the margin, partly concealed by a dark stain. The paper is unevenly sized and contains visible plant fibers, but its surface bears a regular chain-line pattern that seems unusually consistent throughout. Two corrections are written above the line in a different ink; one aligns with the account, while the other appears to alter a total without explanation.

The Vellori Ferry Letter is a single-sheet note attributed in its heading to Marietta Vellori, a Tuscan household secretary, and addressed to her brother Luca in 1492. It was found folded inside a seventeenth-century inventory book in the archive of San Lupo, near the Arno. The text is written in brown iron-gall ink in a sloping humanist cursive, with an abbreviated greeting and a long-tailed “g” resembling forms used in late-fifteenth-century correspondence. Its account of a delayed ferry, a missing coffer, and a request to conceal a packet of household expenses is consistent in tone with practical family letters. The laid paper has a chain-line spacing and a small watermark shaped like a six-petalled flower; a faint address survives on the outer fold. However, the watermark’s central stem appears unusually regular, and the salutation uses a spelling not otherwise found in the letter. A blue pencil shelf mark crosses one edge, while the lower corner is cleanly trimmed.

The Qara-Khuj Toll Ledger is a account sheet said to have been recovered from a sealed storage niche during a survey of a ruined caravan station near the Kulan Pass. It records loads of felt, pepper, and silver ingots, with toll amounts and the names of two caravan leaders, across a sequence of dates attributed to the late eighth century. Most entries are in Sogdian script, while brief numerals and a closing line use a cursive Chinese hand. The thin, buff-colored paper has a central fold, insect losses, and darkening along one edge; several ink strokes appear broken where the sheet is abraded. Its compact abbreviations and alternating scripts resemble features found in other Central Asian trade records, and mineral grains embedded in the paper are consistent with local sediment. However, the paper’s fibers form an unusually even mesh, and a red seal impression includes a border pattern otherwise documented only in later regional material. One cargo term is also written with a character form whose dating is uncertain. No associated container or dated inscription was recovered.

The Reed Gate Register is a six-leaf ritual booklet said to have been recovered in 2019 from a sealed niche behind the altar platform of a disused shrine near the town of Luming. Its text records offerings, invocations, and a sequence for escorting wandering spirits across a boundary marked by reeds. Most passages are written in compact clerical script, with occasional smaller notes in a hand resembling later cursive. The paper is unevenly browned and bears insect holes; a faint fold pattern suggests it was once kept in a narrow wrapper. Several terms for altar officials match forms documented in other Luming records, and the rite’s sequence includes a rare instruction to turn the offering bowl westward. Yet the booklet’s opening title uses a character form not otherwise known from the region, and its final leaf contains a neat red stamp impression whose lettering appears unusually regular. The stitching is intact, though the thread differs from fibers caught in the niche’s wooden seams.

The Gulshan-i-Darbar Leaf is a single-page excerpt from a purported Persian court history of Emperor Jahangir’s seventh regnal year. It was found in 1986 inside a cloth packet in the Mirza Library at Nahrabad, among family papers and unrelated account books. The main text is written in flowing nasta‘liq, with chapter headings in red and a narrow margin of later-looking Persian annotations. Its account of a river crossing names two officers also listed in a separately preserved revenue register, and its honorific formulas resemble those in other period chronicles. The cream paper has visible laid lines, small wormholes, and an irregular edge trimmed close to the text. A faint blue floral watermark appears beneath the final lines; its design resembles motifs used in later paper. The leaf’s brown-black ink has feathered slightly, while the red headings remain unusually bright. A folded lower corner bears a brief note in a different hand and darker ink.

The Life of Drolma Zangpo is a twelve-folio biography of a monk associated with the remote Kharu Monastery in the valley of Nyima Lung. It was found folded inside a wooden document chest beneath a collapsed chapel floor. The text is written mainly in black ink in a compact dbu med hand, with headings and the opening syllables of sections in red. Its account traces Drolma Zangpo’s training, travels, and establishment of a small retreat; several named springs and ridge paths correspond to features recorded on an old estate map from the same valley. The folios are unevenly cut, and their paper contains visible plant fibers and scattered mineral flecks. A closing colophon gives a cyclical year and names a scribe. However, one central folio is a different shade and bears a faint ruled guide beneath the writing. Some spellings vary within the text, and the colophon’s date is partly obscured by a later ink stain.

This single-leaf record purports to be a copy of an entry from the court register of Selimpaşa, dated 1172 AH (1758–59 CE), concerning a tenant’s disputed payment for a riverside mill. It was found folded inside a nineteenth-century bundle of petitions in the imagined Hümayun District Archive. The text is in Ottoman Turkish written in Arabic script, with the plaintiff’s name and the sum entered in a compact, sloping hand. Its opening and closing formulas resemble those used in court records, and the witness list includes titles and occupational terms consistent with the stated setting. The cream-colored paper has scattered iron-gall ink corrosion, a central fold, and pinholes along one edge; a faint laid-line pattern is visible when held to light. However, the paper bears part of a watermark showing a crown above the initials “M.R.,” while the lower margin has a neat red ruling unlike the irregular ruling elsewhere. The date is written over a small patch of scraped fibers, and the clerk’s name appears in a darker ink.

This document consists of nine leaves attributed to a lost gazetteer of Nanpu County, supposedly compiled in the Wanli era. They were found folded inside the lining of a wooden account chest in a disused ancestral hall in Lianzhou Prefecture. The text is written in regular script, with occasional clerical-style forms, and contains entries on county boundaries, schools, flood years, local shrines, and the succession of magistrates. Several place-names match those on a separately preserved tax map, and the flood entry gives a date consistent with a recorded breach in the county embankment. The paper is unevenly sized, browned at the folds, and bears insect holes that cross both text and margins. Yet the leaves use a county seal name not otherwise attested for the period; one official title appears in a form common only later. A faint ruled grid is visible beneath some lines, while the final leaf has a sharply cut edge and a small patch of modern-looking adhesive.

The Aonagi Leaves are three joined sheets attributed to the courtier Minamoto no Kiyosue, covering several days in the fourth month of an otherwise unspecified year. They were found inside a lacquered document box during repairs to the Kurose residence, beneath account papers and a fragment of a screen. The entries combine compact cursive kana with brief passages in sinographic characters, recording a palace audience, rain-damaged garden paths, and the exchange of a poem. The paper is unevenly toned, with insect channels crossing two folds; the ink has browned and faintly bitten into the fibers. A narrow strip pasted along one edge resembles a period repair, and the handwriting shifts naturally between hurried notes and formal phrasing. However, the sheets have a regular chain-line pattern not evident in the other papers from the box. One calendrical expression appears unusually standardized, and a short marginal note uses a kana form absent from the main text. The final line is cut off cleanly, while the reverse bears pale, unreadable brush traces.

The Greyfen Grant is a parchment charter dated to the ninth regnal year of the King Arnulf of Varenne, and records a grant of meadow, woodland, and fishing rights to Saint-Lio Abbey, an otherwise house beside the River Olt. It was found folded inside a later-bound rent roll in the abbey archive at Greyfen. The text is written in brown ink in a compact Carolingian minuscule, with a larger initial and a recognisable grant formula; its witness list and the sequence of named officials are internally consistent. The sheet is unevenly trimmed, bears old fold lines and handling stains, and has two slits at the foot where a pendant seal could have been attached. However, the ink of the final dating clause is darker and slightly more glossy than the main text. Several abbreviations are uncommon, and the clause defining the boundary uses a term otherwise absent from the charter’s vocabulary. No seal survives; a brittle reddish deposit remains near one slit.

The Kumbhavatī Leaf Commentary is a palm-leaf booklet containing a Pali prose gloss on the *Sīhapañha Sutta*, a discourse otherwise unknown in the imagined Kumbhavatī collection. It was recorded in 1912 among roof timbers removed from the abandoned Vejjayanta monastery at Nandapura, a town in the island kingdom of Sīhadvīpa. The leaves bear rounded Sinhala-style characters, with occasional letter forms resembling those in locally dated manuscripts assigned to the twelfth century. Their edges are darkened, and several have old cord holes, insect channels, and repairs made with narrow strips of darker palm. The text’s vocabulary and sandhi are broadly consistent with Pali commentarial prose; a colophon names the monk Dhammakitti and gives a lunar date. Yet the punctuation is unusually systematic, one marginal gloss uses a technical term uncommon in the surrounding passages, and the colophon’s date is written in a different hand. A faint ruled border also appears beneath some incisions.

The Qinghe Stage Leaf is a single folded sheet reportedly recovered in 1936 from a sealed niche beneath the Guanyin Hall at Shuanghe, an abandoned market town in northern Henan. Its text is written chiefly in large, irregular Chinese characters, with smaller interlinear notes and a brief colophon; the hand includes forms associated with Yuan-period vernacular copies. The leaf preserves a scene from a zaju play, naming a judge, a traveling singer, and a drum-and-clapper cue, followed by two lines of song in alternating seven-character and colloquial phrasing. The buff paper has visible plant fibers, uneven sizing, worm channels, and a fold pattern consistent with repeated handling. A narrow strip sewn along one edge bears a repair stitch of dark silk. However, the colophon gives a cyclical date without a reign title, and one song uses a theatrical term otherwise recorded in later playbooks. A pale rectangular stain crosses several characters, while the ink beneath it remains unusually sharp.

The Sela Rule Leaf is a palm-leaf fragment said to have been recovered from a sealed clay jar beneath the floor of the Vejja monastery’s eastern storehouse, during a recorded excavation in 1912. It is written in a compact, right-to-left script locally termed Old Kora, with letter forms resembling those on two stone boundary marks dated, in the monastery’s own calendar, to the fourth century. The leaf preserves portions of rules on communal meals, robe distribution, and procedures for settling disputes; a damaged passage refers to a rainy-season residence near a named river. Its browned surface has insect channels and edge wear, and a cord hole aligns with the surviving groove. The writing fluid has soaked unevenly into the palm. However, the leaf’s unusually narrow dimensions match a later regional format, and one rule uses a technical term otherwise attested only in much later records. A short closing line appears in a visibly different hand, using a spelling absent from the main text.

The North Court Translation Leaf is a single-page Buddhist text fragment recovered from a storage pit beneath the ruined Shuanghe Monastery at Beiyuan. It contains portions of a dialogue on vows, with a short Chinese rendering of a Sanskrit phrase and a colophon naming the translator as the otherwise unattested monk Fajing, in the twelfth year of the Jianhe reign. The main text is written in regular clerical script, while the colophon uses a smaller, more cursive hand. The sheet is brown hemp paper, unevenly trimmed, with insect channels, a folded margin, and dark ink that has feathered into several fibers. A narrow strip of silk remains attached along one edge, and the spacing of the lines is consistent with a hand-copied scroll. However, the colophon uses a compound title also found in later catalogues, and a red seal impression overlaps the text rather than the margin. Fine ruled lines appear beneath the writing.

The Ash-Gate Leaf is a single paper sheet said to have been recovered in 1924 from a sealed cupboard beneath the Heshan Monastery, near the old river crossing at Linyu. It carries a seven-character regulated poem about a night ferry, attributed in a small heading to the otherwise unattested Tang poet Pei Rulan. The main text is written in dark ink in a brisk semi-cursive hand; several characters have forms consistent with early medieval models, while the heading uses a later-looking variant. The buff paper is thin and uneven, with visible plant fibers, a folded center, and a brown water stain that interrupts two lines. Its torn lower edge bears traces of stitching, and the reverse has a faint, partial inventory mark in red. A narrow strip pasted over one damaged corner contains a gloss in a different hand, naming a local ferry station whose recorded name appears in no surviving map. No date or colophon is present.

The Ashen Ford Chronicle is a single parchment leaf describing a disputed succession in the March of Veyr in 1138. It was found in 1896 inside a walled-up cupboard beneath the sacristy of Saint Orlan’s, at the village of Mereholt. The text is in a compact Gothic bookhand, with abbreviated Latin and occasional vernacular place-names. Its account names two otherwise attested local officials and records a toll exemption also listed in a surviving abbey rent roll. The parchment has a crease consistent with long storage folded into a small volume, and its iron-gall ink has browned unevenly. A short passage in the lower margin, however, uses a spelling form not securely documented in the region before the late thirteenth century. The leaf’s ruled lines were drawn with a hard point, while the red initials appear to have been added in a pigment mixture unlike that on nearby service books. No date or scribe’s name appears.

The Luyin Market Leaf is a single printed sheet, reportedly recovered from a sealed storage pit beneath the South Granary at Qingshui Ford. Its colophon gives the date as the third year of the Xianhe reign (1134) and names a local office responsible for issuing market notices. The text, printed in small regular script, lists monthly grain prices, weights, and two brief instructions for reporting shortages. Most characters are cut in a consistent hand, with slight wear at the edges of the impressions; the gray-brown paper has visible plant fibers and uneven thickness. A narrow margin bears a faint vertical crease and traces of what may be old paste. The layout resembles other Song-period single-sheet notices, and one damaged character is corrected by a small inserted block. However, the colophon’s date is set apart by an unusually ornamental frame, several characters use forms uncommon in the body text, and the sheet’s ruling lines are unusually regular. A tiny red seal appears near the lower edge.

The Seiganji Rice Register is a temple account leaf dated 1628, found inside a wooden document chest beneath the storehouse floor of the Kōunji temple in northern Shinano. It records rice rents from seven named hamlets, payments for roof repairs, and a small allotment of candles for a memorial service. The main text is written in running kanji and cursive kana; figures and two later-looking annotations appear in a darker hand. The thin paper has visible kozo fibers, irregularly spaced laid lines, and insect holes that continue across a fold. A vermilion seal partly overlaps the final entry, while its faint border resembles the seal impression on another leaf in the same chest. The date uses an era name appropriate to 1628, and several village names match those on a nearby boundary map. However, one kana form is uncommon in surviving records of that period, and the heading includes a bureaucratic phrase more often documented in later temple accounts. The lower edge is unusually straight and clean.

The Vathyrion Life is a short parchment account of the martyrdom of Saint Eudokia of Kallipetra, a coastal community, preserved in a bundle discovered behind a blocked stair in the monastery of Saint Thalasson on the island of Nerys. Its twelve leaves are written in brown ink, mostly in a compact, right-slanting minuscule, with red initials and occasional marginal signs. The account describes Eudokia’s arrest, a dispute with a provincial official, and a nocturnal vision; its closing prayer names a local spring whose title also appears in a later pilgrim’s itinerary. Several letter forms and the restrained decoration resemble those found in other regional books dated to the eleventh century. Yet the parchment leaves differ noticeably in thickness, and sewing holes do not align consistently. A scraped patch beneath the final prayer carries faint traces of a different line. The title is in a darker ink, and one calendrical expression in the narrative is unusually late in form.

The Seoryeon Votive Plaque is a inscribed stone said to have been recovered in 1987 from the collapsed foundation of Seoryeon Hermitage, an site in the eastern Korean peninsula. The gray granite slab measures 31 by 19 centimeters, with a chipped upper edge, shallow surface scaling, and pale mineral deposits in several cuts. Its 26 lines are written mainly in formal Chinese characters, with two short passages using phonetic glosses to record Korean names. The text dates a dedication to the seventeenth year of King Munjong (1063), lists donors, and requests merit for the dead. Several characters have narrow, uneven strokes resembling hand-cut lettering; the spacing also contracts around a natural fissure. A patch near the lower margin, however, is unusually smooth, and two characters there use forms commonly found in much later inscriptions. The stone’s reported burial position is described as undisturbed, though no sealed excavation record accompanies the account.

The Blue Gate Account is a single paper leaf presented as an excerpt from a register of endowed-property revenues in the town of Qaryat al-Nujum. It was reportedly found folded into the back board of a nineteenth-century copy of the chronicle *Garden of the Two Rivers*, in a storeroom at the town’s old Dār al-Kutub. The main text, in brown ink, is a compact naskh hand, with headings and totals in red; a smaller hand adds brief Arabic notes in the margins. It lists rents from a mill, orchard, and market stalls, naming a trustee and giving a Hijri date equivalent to the early thirteenth century. The thin, buff paper has visible chain lines, an uneven edge, and a water stain crossing two entries. The accounting formulas and abbreviated numerals resemble medieval usage. However, the trustee’s title appears in an unusually late form, and a marginal note uses a spelling associated with modern cataloguing. A faint blue seal overlaps the date.

The Lornavia Ferry Letter is a single-sheet missive addressed to the humanist Pietro Vellori and preserved among the papers of the House of Serevan. It was reportedly found in a sealed cedar chest beneath the choir loft of the former Abbey of Saint Orra, in the town of Bellacorte. The letter discusses a delayed ferry, a payment to a copyist, and the circulation of a small collection of private correspondence. Its Italianate cursive has long descenders and frequent ligatures; several letter forms resemble those used in northern Italian documents of the early sixteenth century. The laid paper bears a faint bell-shaped watermark also recorded on two locally dated account leaves. The sheet is folded into thirds, with an address panel and rusty pinholes along one edge. However, the greeting uses an unusually formal title, and a phrase in the final paragraph appears in later-looking, unusually regular ink. A narrow strip of paper has been pasted over part of the address.

The Vardun Caravan Account is a merchant’s tally, reportedly recovered from a sealed storage niche at the waystation of Vardun, on a branch route between the Oxus and the eastern passes. It is written mainly in cursive Sogdian script on a narrow sheet of light-brown paper, folded into thirds. The text records bolts of dyed cloth, pepper, and two pack animals entrusted to a trader named Naris; sums are entered in the margins, with a short list of creditors below. The sheet has softened fold ridges, scattered pinholes, and darkening along one edge. Ink strokes vary in density, and several numerals overlap older-looking stains. A red-brown seal impression bears a crescent and three dots, though its lines remain unusually sharp against the rubbed paper. The heading gives a date in the “Blue Gate count,” a notation absent from the body, and one commodity is measured in “glass-weights.” A faint later-looking repair strip crosses a torn corner.

The Reed-Gate Register is a Daoist ritual booklet said to have been recovered from a bricked niche beneath the former Cloud-Reed Shrine in the district of Luchuan. It consists of nine folded leaves of pale, uneven paper, with a narrow cord-hole at the outer edge and darkening along the folds. Most lines are written in black ink in a compact, somewhat irregular clerical hand; headings and invocation marks are brushed in cinnabar. The text gives instructions for a rain-stilling offering, names a sequence of spirit officials, and includes a short record of payments in grain and lamp oil. Several ink strokes run into old creases, and a small insect channel passes through two written lines. The paper shows visible plant fibers and scattered inclusions. However, the leaves have unusually uniform dimensions, the cord-hole is cleanly circular, and one repeated seal character has a form otherwise associated in the booklet with a different title. A brief note at the end uses a term not found elsewhere in the text.

The Amber Audience Leaf is a single-page fragment said to have come from a bundle of household papers uncovered in 1912 behind a timber screen in a disused room of a haveli near Amber. It records a court audience during the reign of Emperor Jahangir, naming two provincial officials and noting a petition concerning a disputed garden revenue grant. The main text is in elegant nastaʿliq, with Persian headings and a brief docket in a different hand. Its laid paper has visible chain lines, scattered wheat-straw fibers, and a brown stain consistent with prolonged folding; the ink has penetrated the fibers unevenly. A short phrase in the margin uses a form of an administrative title otherwise documented in later copies, while the emperor’s regnal year is written in an unusual order. The page has a narrow strip pasted along one edge, and its ruling appears to continue beneath it. No matching leaf or original bundle wrapper accompanies the fragment.

The Lharu Life is a short biography of the Tibetan monk Tenzin Drakpa, who is said to have founded a retreat at Khyungdzong Monastery in the eleventh century. It was found folded inside a wooden cabinet during an inventory of the monastery’s north chapel in 1912, between two bundles of ritual notes. The text is written in dark brown ink in a compact dbu med hand on eight uneven sheets of handmade paper. Fibers, insect channels, and a faint crease running through several leaves continue across the joined sheets; the colophon also gives a regnal year consistent with the biography’s stated chronology. Yet the paper’s outer sheet bears a pale blue maker’s mark unlike the other leaves, and a few characters use spellings that appear unusually regular beside the otherwise variable hand. A red seal is impressed over the colophon, while its border is sharply defined and its pigment sits above a later-looking patch of surface sizing.

This document is a single leaf described as a copy of a ruling from the court of the imagined Ottoman district of Sarnıç, dated 1182 AH (1768–69 CE). It was recorded as having been found in a wooden chest during an inventory of the Hacı Selim waqf office. The main text is in Ottoman Turkish, written in a compact hand resembling siyakat, with a short summary in a more legible hand above it. It concerns a dispute over tolls collected at a bridge and names two witnesses, a judge, and a waqf administrator. The phrasing of the witness formula and the order of the parties resemble forms used in other period legal records. The cream-colored paper has laid lines, worn folds, and a small water stain; a brown seal impression is partly legible. However, the date is written in a different ink, the summary uses an administrative title not otherwise mentioned in the ruling, and the seal’s border overlaps the text unusually.

The “Qinghe County Gazetteer Fragment” is a six-leaf section of a purported local gazetteer, found in 2019 inside a wooden chest beneath the floorboards of the Shuangxi Temple, in Qinghe County, Jiangnan. Its paper is unevenly toned, with worm channels that pass through several leaves and a small repaired tear stitched with coarse thread. The text is written mainly in regular script, with occasional running-script annotations. It describes county boundaries, a flood-control embankment, and the annual repair of a shrine to the river god, naming officials and village headmen. Several office titles and administrative terms correspond to forms used in Ming-period records; the account of the embankment also matches the local course of an old, now-buried canal. However, the leaves bear no continuous original pagination, and their binding holes differ in spacing. A colophon gives a compilation date in the Jiajing reign, but its final two characters are written in ink that appears darker and less absorbed than the surrounding text. One annotation uses a phrase otherwise associated with later editions.

The Aoi-no-Tsuyu Diary Leaf is a single folded sheet attributed within its text to Lady Kureha, a attendant at the Heian court, and dated to the fourth month of 1012. It was found in 1926 inside a lacquered document box beneath the floor of a dismantled residence at Kogane Hamlet, near the capital. The paper is thin, unevenly sized, and flecked with short plant fibers; a torn edge bears an old-looking crease and traces of dark adhesive. Most entries combine flowing kana with kanji written in a narrow hand, recording a court excursion, rain at dawn, and the lending of a poem anthology. The ink has browned, and faint offset characters appear on the reverse. A calendar notation fits the stated year, and the paper’s folds align with the box’s dimensions. However, one entry uses a bureaucratic title otherwise documented only in much later records, and the final lines are arranged in unusually regular columns. A pale rectangular stain crosses the date.

The Lorsch Meadow Charter is a one-sheet grant, supposedly issued by a Frankish ruler in 817, transferring meadow rights beside the Weschnitz to a small community associated with the monastery of Saint Arnulf. It was recorded in 1896 among loose papers in a chest in a former mill near Worms; no account of its earlier custody survives. The text is in brown ink on parchment, in a compact minuscule with open a and occasional uncial forms. Its elongated first line and a short formula of royal protection resemble features found in ninth-century grants. The sheet is unusually narrow, however, and its lower edge has been trimmed close to the final line. A faint crease crosses the witness list, where several names are crowded into the margin. The royal monogram is drawn in a different, darker ink, though abrasion may have prompted later reinforcement. The Latin names two local boundaries and a rent of three denarii, but its phrase for the meadow’s annual mowing also occurs in a surviving copy of a charter attributed to the late tenth century.

The Veyyākaraṇa Leaflet is a bundle of nine palm-leaf folios recovered in 1987 from a sealed pottery jar beneath the floor of a ruined storeroom at Kadalivihāra, in the upper Nandā valley. Its text gives an otherwise unattested subcommentary on the *Sammohavinodanī*, including glosses on terms for perception, monastic procedure, and a short parable attributed to the teacher Sīlavanta. The main hand is in a rounded southern Brāhmī-derived script, with several letter forms resembling those in early regional inscriptions. A colophon names the scribe Dhammapāla and gives the year 412 of a local era; the era is not identified. The leaves are darkened and brittle, their string holes worn, and faint ruled lines remain visible. Yet the colophon’s numerals differ from those in the body, and a few glosses use technical vocabulary otherwise attested only in much later works. One leaf also has a small patch of unusually uniform surface polish.

The Willow Ferry Promptbook is a booklet said to have been found inside a timber chest during repairs to the Luyang River shrine in 1986. Its twelve folded leaves contain portions of a zaju play, including role entrances, musical cues, and a comic exchange between a ferryman and a disguised magistrate. Most text is in informal Chinese characters, with red-circle punctuation and occasional small notes in a brisk cursive hand. The dialogue uses several expressions recorded in Yuan-period theatrical glossaries, and the paper’s uneven fibers and insect channels continue across two leaves beneath the binding thread. Yet the booklet’s title appears in a neat running hand unlike the body text, and one cue uses a stage term first attested in a much later repertory list. A pale blue sizing stain lies beneath a pasted repair strip; the strip bears a faint, mirror-reversed fragment of a printed shop mark. The final leaf is missing, leaving a short sequence of cues unfinished.
